# SQL objects: contracts and ownership of logic

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `sql-objects-boundaries` · **SQL Server & Data Engineering** · Catalog level: foundation

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S03-Q004](#S03-Q004)

<p>For a business operation that reads and updates SQL Server data, how would you decide between a stored procedure and application code?</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Choose a database object or application boundary from the operation&#x27;s contract and ownership needs.</p>

<ul>
<li>Compare procedure, function and view contracts through concrete callers.</li>
<li>Trace parameter and trigger behavior within a declared SQL Server scope.</li>
<li>Defend placement of logic using transaction, testing and deployment constraints.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

No catalog prerequisite. Establish the terms and scenario assumptions in the foundation questions before progressing; a published lesson is not evidence that you know them.

<p>When should logic live in a stored procedure rather than application code? Begin with what the different SQL objects expose to callers. Explicit procedure calls and event-driven triggers introduce different dependencies; understanding those contracts makes the eventual ownership decision concrete.</p>

### S03-Q001 · Foundation

<p>Compare stored procedures, functions and views in SQL Server. What contract would callers rely on for each?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q001](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q001)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q001](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q001)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare stored procedures, functions and views.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Compare how each database object is invoked, what it exposes and where it fits in an application. Keep object capabilities separate from assumptions about performance.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Distinguish database object contracts through a concrete calling example.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Establish the SQL Server version and function/view form before making capability claims; check official documentation for those limits.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains the calling contract and ownership for each object.</li>
<li>Chooses an object for an example and names a constraint that could change that choice.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Treating every database object as interchangeable or assuming one is always faster.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would the contract affect testing and changing its callers?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q005"></a>

### S03-Q005 · Mechanism

<p>How does a caller pass parameters to a SQL Server stored procedure and obtain its outputs?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q005](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q005)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q005](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q005)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How are parameters passed to stored procedures?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Trace a call from argument values to the procedure&#x27;s parameter contract and back to the caller. Distinguish different forms of output rather than calling everything a return value.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Explain a procedure call accurately across the application/database boundary.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Specify the SQL Server and .NET provider versions, parameter types and nullability; confirm binding and output behavior in official documentation.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Separates inputs, output parameters, return status and result sets in an example.</li>
<li>Identifies a type or null-handling boundary and describes how to test it.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Treating text concatenation as parameter binding or mixing output channels.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would you inspect if a parameter works in a SQL console but fails in a C# call?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q002"></a>

### S03-Q002 · Application

<p>For a concrete database operation, why would you choose a stored procedure? What requirement would make you reconsider?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q002](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q002)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q002](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q002)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Why would you use a stored procedure?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Make a decision for an operation rather than list generic benefits. Explain what the database interface needs to protect or simplify.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Justify using a stored procedure against an application-side alternative.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use SQL Server and a stated workload; separate desired properties from measured results. Do not assume the procedure improves performance automatically.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Connects the choice to permissions, transaction boundaries or interface ownership.</li>
<li>Names a maintenance cost and an observable way to compare alternatives.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Giving a memorized benefits list without identifying who calls or maintains the procedure.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you deploy a procedure change while older application instances still run?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q003"></a>

### S03-Q003 · Application

<p>When would you expose data through a view rather than let every caller write the underlying query?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q003](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q003)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q003](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q003)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Why would you use a view?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Explain the purpose of a reusable query interface and what it hides from its consumers. Use one reporting or application example.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Choose a view from the consumers&#x27; data contract and maintenance needs.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Discuss an ordinary SQL Server view; indexed-view behavior is a separate, version-sensitive extension. State which columns and rows callers require.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Describes the caller-facing contract and the owner of changes.</li>
<li>Explains how to check correctness and performance instead of assuming the abstraction guarantees either.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Confusing an ordinary view with stored results or promising faster queries without evidence.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What could break consumers when the underlying schema changes?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q006"></a>

### S03-Q006 · Trade-offs

<p>What are database triggers, which types matter in SQL Server, and when would you choose one for a specific requirement?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q006](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q006)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q006](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q006)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What are database triggers, what types exist, and when are they appropriate?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Explain the event that invokes the trigger and the responsibility it takes on. Then justify the choice against an explicit application-side alternative.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Reason about automatic database behavior and its operational consequences.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name the SQL Server version and trigger category; verify supported events and execution behavior in official documentation. State whether an operation affects one or many rows.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces triggering work, resulting changes and the failure boundary.</li>
<li>Addresses multi-row testing, hidden coupling and troubleshooting for the chosen use.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Listing trigger types without explaining who can observe or diagnose the implicit work.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you test a trigger when a single statement changes many rows?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q004"></a>

### S03-Q004 · Production decision

<p>For a business operation that reads and updates SQL Server data, how would you decide between a stored procedure and application code?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q004](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q004)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q004](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q004)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> When should logic live in a stored procedure versus application code?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Choose where the logic belongs from responsibilities and constraints. The question concerns ownership and change as well as the transaction&#x27;s data access.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Defend a placement decision and the condition that changes it.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State the operation, transaction boundary, application callers and teams that deploy each side. No universal placement rule is assumed.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Connects the decision to atomicity, testability and deployment ownership.</li>
<li>Explains a realistic alternative and how to validate the chosen boundary.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Saying all business logic must always live on one side without examining the operation.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would your choice change if two independently deployed applications share this operation?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>Two .NET applications share an inventory operation and a reporting interface in SQL Server. Decide which database objects, if any, own each responsibility and how callers pass data. Explain how a change is tested and deployed while old callers remain active; if proposing a trigger, state its event, multi-row behavior to verify and troubleshooting plan.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Distinguishes object contracts and chooses a location for the example logic.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Defends ownership and transaction boundaries, verifies capability limits and explains test/deployment consequences for each caller.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>No caller contract, concrete operation or change-validation plan is supplied; object names alone do not establish a sound boundary.</p>
